Serving as the 64th Bishop of Rome from 590 until 604, this former Roman prefect sent missionaries to England, including Augustine of Canterbury — who was he?
Pope Gregory I: 64th Bishop of Rome; head of the Roman Catholic Church from AD 590 to 604.
In October 2021, this U.S. assistant secretary for health became the nation's first openly transgender four-star officer across all eight uniformed services — who is she?
Rachel Levine: American public health official (born 1957)
Also called Nagorno-Karabakh, this breakaway state in the South Caucasus governed land internationally recognized as Azerbaijan's until a 2023 offensive emptied it of its people — what was it?
Republic of Artsakh: Breakaway state in the South Caucasus (1991–2023). The conflict erupted into a full-out war in 1992.
A Yale graduate and Harvard Law alum, this former Navy lawyer to SEAL Team One became Florida's 46th governor and briefly ran for the 2024 Republican nomination — who is he?
Ron DeSantis: Governor of Florida since 2019.
Nicknamed "Sam Bahadur" — the Brave — and a Military Cross winner in WWII, he led India's army during the 1971 war with Pakistan and became the country's first field marshal. Which general was he?
Known as 'the eye of Ra,' this Egyptian warrior goddess of medicine is often linked with Hathor and Bastet — who is she?
Sekhmet: Ancient Egyptian goddess. Sekhmet is also a solar deity, sometimes given the epithet "the eye of Ra".
Born in Singapore in 1983, this former Xiaomi finance chief has run a wildly popular ByteDance-owned video app since 2021 — who is he?
Shou Zi Chew: Singaporean business executive (born 1983)
A barrister who founded his own Democratic Party, this politician stepped up after Makarios III's death to lead his Mediterranean island nation as president from 1977 to 1988 — who was he?
Spyros Kyprianou: President of Cyprus from 1977 to 1988.
Led by Alexis Tsipras, who twice served as Greece's prime minister starting in 2015, this pro-European left-wing coalition was founded in 2004 — which party?
Syriza: Political party in Greece. It was founded in 2004 as a political coalition of left-wing and radical left parties, and registered as a political party in 2012.
The eldest son of a US president, this brigadier general received the Medal of Honor for directing troops at Utah Beach during the Normandy landings — who is he?
Theodore Roosevelt Jr.: American general and politician (1887–1944)
Born a peasant, this man rose to become the most powerful figure in Japan and the first person ever to hold the rank of Kampaku without being born a noble — who was this second 'Great Unifier'?
Toyotomi Hideyoshi: Military ruler of Japan from 1585 to 1598.
Composed in an archaic Sanskrit dialect, this collection of four ancient hymn texts forms the oldest layer of Hindu scripture — what are they collectively called?
A former Fudan University law-school dean and professor of international politics, he became a leading Communist Party ideologist and now chairs the CPPCC — which Chinese politician?

Serving as both the last prime minister of Great Britain and the first of the United Kingdom, this statesman held office through the French Revolution and Napoleonic Wars, and was distinguished from his father, who shared his surname — who was he?
William Pitt the Younger: British statesman (1759–1806)
This Korean admiral won all of his roughly 23 naval battles against Japan, most famously defeating a fleet of over 130 ships with just 13 of his own — who is he?
Often called the 'Bismarck of Japan' for his realpolitik nation-building, this Satsuma-born statesman was one of three nobles who led the 1868 Meiji Restoration — who is he?
Who among these was born first?
Christine Ladd-Franklin (born 1847) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these was born first?
Stephen Hales (born 1677) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these four appeared first?
Pascal (programming language) (published 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Pierre Curie is a physicist. Pierre Curie (15 May 1859 – 19 April 1906) was a French physicist and chemist, and a pioneer in crystallography and magnetism.
Which of these four is a chemist?
Mario Molina is a chemist. Mario José Molina-Pasquel Henríquez (19 March 1943 – 7 October 2020) was a Mexican physical chemist.
What is the atomic number of Hydrogen?
Hydrogen is a chemical element; it has the symbol H and atomic number 1.
In what year was Hans Albert Einstein born?
Hans Albert Einstein (May 14, 1904 – July 26, 1973) was a Swiss-American engineer, the second child and first son of physicists Albert Einstein and Mileva Marić.
In what year was Mahmoud Ahmadinejad born?
Mahmoud Ahmadinejad (né Sabbaghian; born 28 October 1956) is an Iranian politician who served as the sixth president of Iran from 2005 to 2013.
In what year was Kitty O'Neil born?
Kitty O'Neil: O'Neil subsequently moved into car racing and became a pioneering woman in the stunt industry in Hollywood.
In what year did Blaise Pascal die?
Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 – 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
In what year did Milton Friedman die?
Milton Friedman: Friedman's challenges to what he called "naive Keynesian theory" began with his interpretation of consumption, which tracks how consumers spend.
In what year was Penicillin discovered?
Penicillin was discovered in 1928 by the Scottish physician Alexander Fleming as a crude extract of P. rubens.
In what year was Coulomb's law discovered?
Coulomb's law: This electric force is conventionally called the electrostatic force or Coulomb force.
Which company manufactures Eurocopter AS350 Écureuil?
Eurocopter AS350 Écureuil: Airbus Helicopters. The AS355 Ecureuil 2 is a twin-engine variant, marketed in North America as the TwinStar.
In which country is Junkers Ju 52?
Junkers Ju 52: Germany. Development of the Ju 52 commenced in the late 1920s, headed by German aeronautical engineer Ernst Zindel.
Who is credited with discovering Indium?
Indium: Ferdinand Reich. Indium is a chemical element; its symbol is In and its atomic number is 49.
Who is credited with discovering Californium?
Californium: Stanley Gerald Thompson. Californium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cf and atomic number 98.
Who is credited with discovering Fluorine?
Fluorine: Henri Moissan. Fluorine is a chemical element; it has symbol F and atomic number 9.
This is the most common genetic cause of dwarfism, typically producing short arms and legs with a normal-length torso and an enlarged head with a prominent forehead — what condition is it?
Achondroplasia is a genetic disorder whose primary feature is dwarfism.
The twelfth-brightest star in our night sky and the brightest in the constellation Aquila. It's one of the three vertices of the Summer Triangle asterism. Name this star.

Altair is the brightest star in the equatorial constellation of Aquila and the twelfth-brightest star in the night sky. It has the Bayer designation Alpha Aquilae, which is Latinised from α Aquilae and abbreviated Alpha Aql or α Aql.
This British-American theoretical physicist at the University of Illinois reshaped our understanding of superfluid helium, work crowned by the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physics — who was he?
Anthony Leggett (26 March 1938 - 8 March 2026) was a British-American theoretical physicist and professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC).
With atomic number 85 and symbol At, this is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust, forming only as a decay product of heavier elements — name it?
Astatine is a chemical element; it has symbol At and atomic number 85.
Recorded in an ancient Chinese herbal medicine text from around 200 BC and named for a barberry-related plant genus, this yellow-pigmented alkaloid glows under ultraviolet light. What compound is it?
Berberine is an organic compound classified as benzylisoquinoline alkaloid.
This Russian mathematician-turned-oligarch was worth an estimated $3 billion in 1997 after privatizing state assets like Channel One — yet died impoverished and depressed in 2013. Who was he?
Boris Berezovsky (businessman) (23 January 1946 - 23 March 2013), also known as Platon Elenin, was a Russian business oligarch, government official, engineer and mathematician.
Atomic number 20 and chemically akin to strontium and barium, this metal is the most common ingredient in limestone — found there as its carbonate. What element?
Calcium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ca and atomic number 20.
A first-generation cephalosporin that can be swallowed rather than infused, this antibiotic disrupts the bacterial cell wall to treat ear, skin and urinary infections — what is it?
Cefalexin is an antibiotic that can treat a number of bacterial infections. It kills gram-positive and some gram-negative bacteria by disrupting the growth of the bacterial cell wall.
Charted in 1756 by Lacaille and named for the drafting tool that draws circles, this faint southern constellation is easily confused with the mariner's-compass constellation Pyxis. Which one is it?
Circinus is a small, faint constellation in the southern sky, first defined in 1756 by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille.
First created in Germany in 1996 and named for an astronomer on his 537th birthday, this synthetic element (number 112) may even be a gas — which one?
Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cn and atomic number 112.

Known for names like thornapple, jimsonweed, and devil's trumpet, this genus of nine extremely poisonous, night-blooming plants in the nightshade family can cause hallucinations and delirium if ingested — what is it?
Datura is a genus of nine species of highly poisonous, vespertine-flowering plants belonging to the nightshade family (Solanaceae).
Its name comes from the Ancient Greek for 'female dragon,' and this genus of roughly 200 tree and shrub species now also includes what was once classified as Sansevieria — which genus is it?
Dracaena (plant) is a genus of about 200-220 species of trees and woody shrubs.
What medical condition, caused by viruses like herpes simplex or rabies, bacteria, or autoimmune disease, refers to inflammation of the brain and can cause confusion, seizures, and memory problems?

Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain. The severity can be variable with symptoms including reduction or alteration in consciousness, aphasia, headache, fever, confusion, a stiff neck, and vomiting.
Despite its name, this highly sociable oceanic dolphin earned its label from a skull resembling the orca's — it can reach 20 feet and even forms mixed pods with bottlenose dolphins. What is it?
False killer whale (Pseudorca crassidens) is a species of oceanic dolphin that is the only extant representative of the genus Pseudorca.
He worked on uranium enrichment during the Manhattan Project, then — after McCarthyism cost him his physics post — founded San Francisco's hands-on Exploratorium museum; who was he?

Frank Oppenheimer (August 14, 1912 - February 3, 1985) was an American particle physicist, cattle rancher, professor of physics at the University of Colorado, and the founder of the Exploratorium in San Francisco.

A 1946 civilian demonstrator version of this British fighter became the world's first civilian-registered jet aircraft, decades after it debuted as the Allies' sole combat jet of World War II — which aircraft?
Gloster Meteor was the first British jet fighter and the Allies' only jet aircraft to engage in combat operations during the Second World War.
Caused by a group of enteroviruses, this common infection opens with a fever and then sprinkles blistering spots on exactly the three body parts named in its label. What is it?
Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is a common infection caused by a group of enteroviruses. It typically begins with a fever and feeling generally unwell.
Originally a variable measure equal to one-twelfth of the night or day in the ancient Near East, this unit of time is now fixed at exactly 3,600 seconds — name this unit?
Hour (symbol: h; also abbreviated hr) is a unit of time historically reckoned as 124 of a day and defined contemporarily as exactly 3,600 seconds.
This contagious bacterial skin infection most often shows up as yellowish crusts on a child's face, arms, or legs, and spreads easily in crowded day cares and contact sports — what is it?
Impetigo is a contagious bacterial infection that involves the superficial skin.
This French mathematician of algebraic topology and number theory pulled off a rare double: the Fields Medal in 1954 and, nearly fifty years later, the very first Abel Prize. Who was he?
Jean-Pierre Serre (born 15 September 1926) is a French mathematician who has made contributions to algebraic topology, algebraic geometry and algebraic number theory.
This pain-relieving, fever-reducing drug belongs to the propionic acid class of anti-inflammatories and hit the market in 1980, thirteen years after being patented — what is it?
Ketoprofen is one of the propionic acid class of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) with analgesic and antipyretic effects.
With about 180,000 described species — roughly 10% of all known living organisms — which insect order is the second largest, trailing only the beetles?
Lepidoptera are an order of winged insects which include butterflies and moths.
This programming language, whose bytecode interpreter is written in ANSI C, was created in 1993 mainly to let developers extend and customize software — which language?
Lua is a lightweight, high-level, multi-paradigm programming language designed mainly for embedded use in applications.
Born in 1984, this programmer co-founded a social network at Harvard in 2004 with his roommates and became the world's youngest self-made billionaire by age 23 — who is he?
Mark Zuckerberg (born May 14, 1984) is an American businessman and programmer who co-founded the social media service Facebook and its parent company Meta Platforms.
This medical condition is diagnosed when the erect length of the affected organ measures at least two and a half standard deviations below the average size for age — what condition is it?
Micropenis is an unusually small penis.
Named for the strong odor males emit during rut to attract mates, this thick-coated Arctic hoofed mammal is called 'the bearded one' in Inuktitut — what's the species?
Muskox (Ovibos moschatus) is a hoofed mammal of the family Bovidae.
A highly corrosive mineral compound with the formula HNO3, this strong inorganic acid is colorless but yellows over time as it decomposes. What is this acid?
Nitric acid is an inorganic compound with the formula HNO3. The compound is colorless, but samples tend to acquire a yellow cast over time due to decomposition into oxides of nitrogen.

Believed to be the world's fourth-leading cause of disability, this condition wears down joint cartilage over years, often first striking the knuckles nearest your fingertips and the base of the thumb — what is it?
Osteoarthritis is a type of degenerative joint disease that results from breakdown of joint cartilage and underlying bone.
This species of hickory tree, native to the Mississippi River region of the southern US and northern Mexico, is the official state nut of five states and the state tree of Texas. What nut is this?
Pecan (pih-KAN,; Carya illinoinensis) is a species of hickory native to the Southern United States and northern Mexico in the region of the Mississippi River.
Someone who specializes in matter, motion, and force through space and time earns the title 'physicist' — so what is the field they devote themselves to?
Physics is the scientific study of matter, its fundamental constituents, its motion and behavior through space and time, and the related entities of energy and force.
A strongly alkaline, water-soluble salt of carbonic acid, which compound with the formula K2CO3 is used in glassmaking and Dutch-process chocolate?
Potassium carbonate is the inorganic compound with the formula K2CO3. It is deliquescent, often appearing as a damp or wet solid.
This set of three positive whole numbers, like (3, 4, 5), satisfies a squared plus b squared equals c squared and forms the side lengths of a right triangle — what is it called?
Pythagorean triple consists of three positive integers a, b, and c, such that a2 + b2 = c2.
Beyond his Nobel-winning work in quantum electrodynamics, he explained the superfluidity of supercooled liquid helium and built the parton model — which physicist?
Richard Feynman (May 11, 1918 - February 15, 1988) was an American theoretical physicist.
This Indian-American executive succeeded Steve Ballmer as CEO of a major tech company in 2014 after running its cloud and enterprise division — who is he?
Satya Nadella (born 19 August 1967) is an Indian-American business executive.

Developed by the Chukchi people in the Russian Far East for pulling sleds and companionship, this medium-sized Spitz-family dog breed is smaller than the similar-looking Alaskan Malamute — name the breed?
Siberian Husky is a breed of medium-sized working sled dog.

Distinguished from relatives in its conifer family by four-sided needles attached singly to small peg-like structures on the twigs, this genus of about 37 evergreen tree species thrives across the Northern Hemisphere's boreal forests — what's the tree?

Spruce is a tree of the genus Picea, a genus of some 37 species of coniferous evergreen trees in the family Pinaceae, found in the northern temperate and boreal (taiga) regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
This West African berry contains a molecule that binds so powerfully to taste buds that sour foods eaten afterward taste sweet instead — what's this plant's common nickname?
Synsepalum dulcificum is a plant in the Sapotaceae family, native to tropical Africa.

This weakly radioactive silvery metal, atomic number 90, tarnishes olive-grey in air, and its most stable isotope has a half-life of about 14 billion years — roughly the age of the universe. What element is this?
Thorium is a chemical element; it has symbol Th and atomic number 90.

Entering Soviet service in the 1960s, this jet was the USSR's first supersonic bomber to reach production, though it disappointed with poor range and proved notoriously hard to fly — what aircraft is it?
Tupolev Tu-22 (Air Standardization Coordinating Committee name: Blinder) was the first supersonic bomber to enter production in the Soviet Union.

Many of these carrion-eating birds sport a bald head that stays clean while feeding and helps with temperature control — and they'll even urinate on their own legs to cool off. What kind of bird is it?
Vulture is a bird of prey that scavenges on carrion.
Each individual's coat is unique, and the best evidence suggests their black-and-white pattern wards off biting flies — which striped African equine is this?
Zebra (subgenus Hippotigris) are African equines with distinctive black-and-white striped coats.
Located behind the nasal cavity where the nose meets the throat, which mass of lymphoid tissue is also known as the pharyngeal tonsil?
Adenoid: Type of tonsil. The adenoid, also known as the pharyngeal tonsil, or nasopharyngeal tonsil is the superior-most of the tonsils.

Born out of wedlock in the Caribbean and orphaned young, this Founding Father became the first U.S. secretary of the treasury and started America's first political party, the Federalist Party — who was he?
This memory disorder comes in two main forms — one blocking recall of events before a specific date, the other preventing new experiences from becoming lasting memories — what is it?
Amnesia: Cognitive disorder where memory is disturbed or lost.
Known by the symbol Sb and mined chiefly from stibnite ore, which element has long been powdered into the cosmetic kohl and today hardens lead in car batteries?
Antimony: Chemical element with atomic number 51 (Sb)
Unlike its counterpart which returns blood to the heart, this blood vessel usually carries oxygen-rich blood away from it — what is it?
Artery: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart.
Best known for pioneering radical behaviorism at Harvard, this psychologist invented a chamber for studying operant conditioning that came to bear his name — who is he?
B. F. Skinner: American psychologist and social philosopher (1904–1990)
Built atop an Ilyushin transport and nicknamed 'Mainstay,' this Soviet radar plane had its existence leaked to the West by a spy in 1978 — which aircraft is it?
Beriev A-50: Soviet airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft.
This North American wild cat earns its name from the black-tipped, stubby tail it sports, along with distinctive black bars on its forelegs — one of the four species of lynx. Which animal is it?
Bobcat: Medium-sized North American wild cat.

After resigning from Evergreen State College following 2017 protests over campus racial equity, this podcaster and former evolutionary biology professor was named part of the 'intellectual dark web' — who is he?
Bret Weinstein: American podcaster and author (born 1969)
This highly soluble white crystalline salt is spread on icy roads for de-icing and, in its anhydrous form, works as a moisture-absorbing desiccant. What compound is it?
Calcium chloride: Chemical compound. The compound is a white crystalline solid at room temperature, and it is highly soluble in water.
Native to the Mediterranean, this legume tree's seed pods are ground into a chocolate substitute, while its seeds yield a common food thickener known as locust bean gum — which tree?
Carob: Small tree grown for its edible pods and landscaping.
This goat-antelope roams mountain ranges from the Pyrenees to the Caucasus and has even been introduced to New Zealand's South Island — which animal?
Named after a 17th-century English physician, this ring-shaped network of arteries supplies blood to the brain in humans and other vertebrates — what is it called?
Circle of Willis: Circulatory anastomosis that supplies blood to the brain and surrounding structures.
Also known as foremilk or historically as 'beestings,' this early substance produced by mammary glands right after birth delivers antibodies and immune factors to newborns. What is it?
Colostrum: Form of milk produced immediately following the delivery of newborn.
Latin for 'raven,' this widely distributed bird genus includes crows and rooks and gave a group of its members the eerie collective noun 'a murder' — what genus is it?
Corvus: Genus of birds including crows, ravens and rooks.

First synthesized in 1874, this insecticide earned its discoverer a 1948 Nobel Prize and was used in WWII against malaria and typhus before becoming infamous for its environmental damage — what is it?
DDT: Organochloride known as an insecticide.

This group of microalgae generates roughly a fifth to a half of Earth's oxygen each year, and its dead shells drift on Saharan winds to fertilize the entire Amazon basin with millions of tons of dust annually. What are they?
Diatom: Single-celled alga with a silica cell wall.
Smaller and shorter-necked than their swan and goose cousins in the family Anatidae, these aquatic birds are often confused with grebes, loons, and coots — what are they?
Duck: Common name for many species of bird.
The second-largest member of the deer family, this animal is also called "wapiti," a Shawnee and Cree word meaning "white rump" for the pale fur it flashes to signal alarm — what animal is it?
Elk: Species of deer. The word "elk" originally referred to the European variety of the moose, Alces alces, but was transferred to Cervus canadensis by North American colonists.

In 2019 this French-American MIT economist shared the Nobel with her husband and Michael Kremer for an experimental approach to fighting global poverty, rooted in the randomized trials of her J-PAL lab — who is she?
First confirmedly detected in 1992 orbiting a pulsar, this term describes any planet found outside our solar system — what is it?
Exoplanet: Planet outside of the Solar System. The first confirmed detection of an exoplanet was in 1992 around a pulsar, and the first detection around a main-sequence star was in 1995.
From the Latin word for 'tube' or 'pipe,' this medical term describes an abnormal connection between two hollow spaces in the body — what is it?
Fistula: Abnormal connection between two hollow bodily spaces, often organs.
This mathematical principle links differentiation and integration, showing the two operations to be essentially inverses of each other — what is it called?
Fundamental theorem of calculus: Relationship between derivatives and integrals.
The largest of its family, this mostly solitary mammal uses long foreclaws to dig into nests and a sticky tongue to slurp up ants and termites — what animal is it?
Giant anteater: Species of mammal. The giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is an insectivorous mammal native to Central and South America.
Dating back roughly 250 million years to the early Triassic, this ground-dwelling insect hears through an organ on its abdomen and leaps away from danger using powerful hind legs — what is it?
Grasshopper: Common name for a group of insects.

This Austrian physician who coined "autistic psychopathy" lent his name to a syndrome, but later faced allegations he referred disabled children to a Vienna clinic that killed hundreds during the Nazi era — who was he?

First synthesized in 1940 by chemist Roger Adams via hydrogenation of THC isomers, this psychoactive cannabis-derived compound is sold in vaporizers despite never being drug-approved — which compound?
Lightest and most abundant element in the universe, it makes up about 75% of all normal matter and fuels the stars — colorless, odorless, and highly combustible. What element is it?
Hydrogen: Chemical element with atomic number 1 (H)
This contagious bacterial skin infection — usually from Staph or Strep — most often shows up as yellowish crusts on the face, arms or legs. What's it called?
Appointed FBI director by Barack Obama in 2013, this former federal prosecutor was fired from the post in 2017 — who is he?
Nicknamed "Marvellous Merchiston," this 16th-century Scottish laird discovered logarithms and popularized the decimal point — who was this mathematical wizard?

He coauthored the classic 1973 textbook Gravitation, advised Carl Sagan on wormholes for the novel Contact, and shared the 2017 Nobel Prize for the LIGO detection of gravitational waves — which astrophysicist?
Kip Thorne: American physicist, writer, and Nobel Laureate (born 1940)
Closely related to earthworms but equipped with a sucker at each end, these segmented worms are mostly freshwater dwellers, and the medicinal species famously feeds on blood — what are they?
Leech: Parasitic or predatory annelid worms.
A Chinese computer engineer turned science-fiction author, he won the Hugo Award for The Three-Body Problem and the Locus Award for its sequel, Death's End. Who is he?
Liu Cixin: Chinese science fiction writer (born 1963)
Developed by MathWorks and named for its focus on matrix manipulations, this proprietary numeric computing environment powers the add-on Simulink for model-based design. What's it called?
MATLAB: Numerical computing environment and programming language.
Co-founding a company in his Harvard dorm room in February 2004, he became the world's youngest self-made billionaire at age 23. Who is he?
Mark Zuckerberg: American businessman and programmer (born 1984)
Long before chemists called it 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenethylamine, this psychedelic was drawn from peyote and San Pedro cacti for spiritual ceremonies — which naturally occurring compound is it?
Mescaline: Naturally occurring psychedelic compound. The practice of ingesting mescaline-containing cacti extracts dates back over 6,000 years.

Codenamed 'Havoc' by NATO, this Soviet tandem-seat attack helicopter carries a single gun in an under-nose barbette and, unlike its predecessor, has no secondary troop-transport role. What aircraft is this?
Mil Mi-28: Russian attack helicopter. The Mil Mi-28 (NATO reporting name "Havoc") is a Soviet heavy-weight, all-weather, day-night, tandem-seat anti-armour military attack helicopter.

This Japanese biologist used diffusion equations to calculate how likely a gene is to take over a population, and in 1968 proposed the "neutral theory" that genetic drift, not just selection, drives molecular evolution — who was he?
Also called the belly button, this flat or hollowed spot on the abdomen marks where the umbilical cord once attached — what is it?
Navel: Scarred area on the abdomen after detachment of the umbilical cord.
Nicknamed the 'winter vomiting disease' and spread by the fecal-oral route, this is the most common cause of gastroenteritis — what is it?
Norovirus: Type of viruses that cause gastroenteritis.

Numbering 126 species, these are the largest order of marsupials in the Western Hemisphere — and only one of them, the Virginia variety, made it as far north as the United States and Canada. What animal is this?
Nicknamed the 'white rats' of its phylum for how often it's cultivated in classrooms and labs, this single-celled ciliate thrives in stagnant ponds — what is it?
Known for its speed, this large crow-sized raptor has a blue-grey back, barred white underparts, and a black head — an avivore with marked sexual dimorphism — what is it?
Peregrine falcon: Fastest known animal and common bird of prey.
This branch of biology studies how organs, cells, and biomolecules carry out their functions, and gives its name, alongside medicine, to a Nobel Prize category — which field?
Physiology: Science regarding functions in organisms or living systems.
First domesticated some 5,000 years ago on the Iranian plateau, this fruit-bearing shrub reached California in 1769 via Spanish settlers — which fruit?
Pomegranate: Fruit-bearing deciduous shrub. Pomegranate was first domesticated by ancient Iranians in the Iranian plateau and nearby regions about 5,000 years ago.
This thorny European shrub's tart fruit gives sloe gin its name in Britain, while its wood becomes the classic Irish walking stick — what is it?
Prunus spinosa: Species of flowering plant in the rose family.
Domesticated in Asia, this crunchy root vegetable in the mustard family owes its peppery bite to compounds like glucosinolate — what vegetable is it?
Radish: Root vegetable of the Brassicaceae family. The radish (Raphanus sativus or Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. sativus) is a flowering plant in the mustard family, Brassicaceae.
Named from Greek words for 'rose' and 'tree,' this flowering shrub genus is Nepal's national flower and includes azaleas as a subgenus — which plant?
Rhododendron: Genus of flowering plants. Azaleas make up two subgenera of Rhododendron.
This Japanese botanist lived and worked during the Meiji era of the late 19th century — who was he?
Ryōkichi Yatabe: Japanese botanist and poet. Ryōkichi Yatabe (矢田部良吉; October 13, 1851 – August 8, 1899) was a Japanese botanist during the Meiji era.
Sitting near the center of the Milky Way between Libra and Sagittarius, this zodiac constellation's recognition predates ancient Greek culture — which constellation?
Scorpius: Zodiac constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere.
Resembling a long-nosed mouse but actually a closer relative of hedgehogs and moles, this small mammal has sharp spike-like teeth rather than gnawing incisors — what is it?
Mostly made from potato starch but also found in apples and berries, this slowly-metabolized sugar alcohol is an isomer of mannitol, differing only at one hydroxyl group. What is it?
Common in coastal tropical waters worldwide, this group of cartilaginous fish includes about 220 species across 29 genera, from butterfly rays to manta and devil rays — what are they?

Located near the border of two constellations some 18.2 billion light-years away, this hyperluminous quasar harbors one of the most massive black holes ever found, at roughly 40 billion solar masses — what is it?
TON 618: Quasar and Lyman-alpha blob in the constellations of Canes Venatici and Coma Berenices.
Discovered via its telltale green spectral line in 1861, this silvery post-transition metal takes its name from the Greek word for a green shoot — which element?
Thallium: Chemical element with atomic number 81 (Tl)
Called the "Father of Japanese Botany," this grammar-school dropout collected over 500,000 plant specimens and earned a doctorate — and his birthday is now Botany Day in Japan. Who was he?
Also known as 45,X, which chromosomal condition affects only females who are born with a single X chromosome instead of two, often causing short stature and a webbed neck?
Turner syndrome: X chromosome monosomy. Small chin (micrognathia), loose folds of skin on the neck, slanted eyelids and prominent ears are found in Turner syndrome, though not all will show it.
